title.en: Review: serving with the mind alone

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous chapter: Chochmah and Binah meditating on Hashem's greatness should stir love and fear in the heart, but one who cannot may serve with the mind's understanding alone. Such a soul is still 'in the womb' of Knesses Yisroel and not yet 'born', so revealed love is not required of it.

title.en: Chapter 17 and the verse 'ki karov'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that chapter 17 begins a new phase, applying the earlier axioms in practice, and that the title page names the verse 'ki karov eilecha' as the Tanya's purpose. He raises the difficulty that our senses seem to deny it, and rejects the idea that it applied only to Moshe Rabbeinu's generation: the Torah speaks to every generation and every person.

title.en: Love cannot be divided

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why turning the heart from worldly desire to true love of Hashem is so hard: love is indivisible and can be directed to only one object. With the example of enjoying an ice cream, he says that one who still desires worldly pleasure and thinks he also loves Hashem is imagining it, though thinking of Hashem while eating is better than nothing.

title.en: Tzaddikim beyond the taste of food

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Ba'al HaTanya and his chassidim experienced this level, and tells of tzaddikim in recent times: one who said he had not known the taste of food for twenty years, two Rebbes recalling the wartime transports, and the Yismach Moshe, who ate dishwater thinking it was soup. He ends that one who still enjoys the ice cream should not fool himself that his love of Hashem is complete.

title.en: 'Yirah is a small thing' for Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that calls yirah a small thing for Moshe Rabbeinu, and explains that a complete transformation of the heart belongs to tzaddikim like Dovid HaMelech, not to beinonim. What Hashem asks of everyone, as the previous chapters explained, is enough yirah in the mind to drive the doing.

title.en: Doing the mitzvah from the mind's duty

summary.en: The Mashgiach stresses that the Tanya does not say to refrain from the ice cream; it says that when a mitzvah comes, the mind should recognize the duty and act. His example is tefillin: one may not feel the glow, but feels the obligation because Hashem requires it, and this suffices for a soul from ibbur rather than leidah.

title.en: Logical love is in every person's power

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the level near to everyone is a logical love, even if it is not revealed in the heart like flames of fire, because the mind is in a person's power: he cannot love as he wishes but can think as he wishes. He compares it to a mother's love that she does not always feel, and says the felt joy of the mitzvah is its reward, granted to tzaddikim but not required of everyone in this world.

title.en: The mind rules the heart, except in a rasha

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that by nature the mind controls the heart, the mouth and the limbs, except in a true rasha, who has lost that control; he brings Chazal that the wicked are in the power of their heart and the heart of tzaddikim is in their power, and the question of Pharaoh's hardened heart. He explains the loss of control as a punishment that began with free choice, comparing it to a case in the Gemara that starts with negligence and ends with compulsion, and concludes that 'ki karov' does not speak to such reshaim, who are called dead in their lifetime.

title.en: How a rasha begins: a broken heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how one who lost his free choice can do teshuvah, and answers that every Jew has a point that evil cannot touch, which Hashem sometimes arouses through circumstances. A rasha can do a mitzvah here and there, but to begin real service he must first break the iron wall of the kelipos with a broken heart; this is the lower teshuvah, as opposed to the higher teshuvah from love.

title.en: Raising the fallen Hei; Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sin separates the lower Hei, the Shechinah, from the Name, dragging it into exile with the person, and teshuvah, 'tashuv Hei', returns it. He connects this to Chanukah of the coming month Kislev: the wicks and oils that do not burn on Shabbos burn on Chanukah, since then Hashem comes down to lift the fallen; he ends with the Tanya's description of the rasha's soul in exile.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach tells stories of Rebbes, among them a Rebbe who spent a night in a Vienna jail with a broken Jew and understood only years later, in America, why he had been there.

abstract.en: In this short shiur the Mashgiach tells a few stories, apparently about the Kapishnitzer Rebbe. He first describes a chuppah where several Rebbes were present and the Skverer Rebbe asked that the Satmar Rebbe, Reb Yoel, be called up for a brachah. He then tells of a father whose son was involved with a non-Jewish girl and who made an engagement party with much liquor, where the drunk guests began to insult Jews. The main story follows: the Rebbe was held one night in a jail in Vienna, and a Jew who had married out many years before was brought in and spent the night in anguish, crying out. The Rebbe was freed the next morning without understanding why he had to be there; only years later in America, when that Jew came to him with his son, did he understand.

en: At a chuppah where several Rebbes were present, the Skverer Rebbe asked that the Satmar Rebbe, Reb Yoel, be called up for a brachah.
A Rebbe spent one night in a Vienna jail, where a Jew who had married out many years before spent the night crying out in anguish.
Freed the next morning, the Rebbe did not understand why he had to be there; only in America, when the Jew came to him with his son, did he understand.

title.en: Stories of Rebbes and a night in jail

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a chuppah attended by several Rebbes, tells of an engagement party where drunk guests insulted Jews, and then tells of a Rebbe's night in a Vienna jail with a Jew who had married out, whose purpose he understood only years later in America.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's emunah is a feeling of the heart inherited from the mother, so that even a Jewish apikorus believes deep down and only invents excuses, like the fox with his 'sour grapes'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by contrasting a goy, who can grasp emunah through logic, with a Jew, who senses it by instinct. He illustrates instinct with the Chasam Sofer on a father who breaks into his son's home unaware: the son may not kill him, since the father's heart knows. Jews are Hashem's children and feel Him with the heart. The three matzos and four cups at the Seder stand for the Avos and the Imahos, mind and heart. A disciple feels his Rebbe, as the Lechovitcher felt the passing of Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin. Jewishness follows the mother because emunah, a feeling, comes from her, which the Mashgiach also reads in the word emunah itself. Using Ben Sira's fable of the fox and the sour grapes, he shows how gaavah drives a person to justify himself: Esav blamed his wives, and the Jewish apikorus, who truly believes, denies only to follow his desires.

en: A goy can understand emunah through logic, but a Jew senses it by instinct, with his heart.
Just as a father's heart senses his son even when he does not know it is him, Jews, as Hashem's children, feel a bond with Him that goes beyond what the mind dictates.
The three matzos and four cups correspond to the Avos and Imahos: chochmah, the mind, and binah, the feeling of the heart, in which women are greater.
A child's Jewishness follows the mother because emunah is a feeling, and feeling comes from the mother.
Out of gaavah a person refuses to admit his own failure and blames something else, as the fox called the grapes sour.
A Jewish apikorus truly believes deep in his heart; he denies only because he wants to follow his desires.

title.en: A Jew's emunah is instinct

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts a goy, who understands emunah through logic, with a Jew, who senses it by instinct. He brings the Chasam Sofer on a father who breaks into his son's home unaware that it is his son's: the son may not kill him, since the father's heart knows. The same feeling exists in animals, and Jews, as Hashem's children, feel Him with the heart.

title.en: Matzos and cups: mind and heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three matzos are the Avos and the four cups the Imahos, chochmah and binah. Facts of the mind are the same for everyone, while the heart leans by a person's nature, as with Beis Hillel. He brings that women were given extra binah, that grain gives understanding while wine stirs feeling, and ties this to the two shins of the tefillin and to the emunah in the heart inherited from Avraham.

title.en: The feeling of a wife and a disciple

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why one witness suffices to let a woman remarry: she feels whether her husband is alive. So too a disciple feels his bond to his Rebbe, and he tells how the Lechovitcher cried out that he no longer felt his Rebbe until he was told that Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin had passed away.

title.en: Why Jewishness follows the mother

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a child's Jewishness is set by the mother when tribe and inheritance follow the father, and answers that emunah is a feeling, which comes from the mother. He then shows it in loshon hakodesh: when a verb ending in nun becomes a noun, the last nun falls away, as chanun becomes chen, shanun becomes shen and ganun becomes gan; so amun becomes em, mother.

title.en: Ben Sira's fable of the sour grapes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's discussion of Ben Sira, who wrote fables of foxes that the nations later took over. He tells the fable of the fox who struggled for three days to climb a fence to reach grapes and then declared them sour, and explains that a person, out of gaavah, would rather blame the grapes than admit his own weakness.

title.en: Esav blames his wives

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates that the Chazon Ish told a melamed who wanted to study psychology that everything can be learned from Chumash and Rashi. He then shows the same trait in the parsha: Esav saw that he lost the brachos and that Yaakov was sent to take a proper wife, concluded that his wives were to blame, and married the daughter of Yishmael, rather than admitting his own fault.

title.en: Rationalization and the Jewish apikorus

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives examples of blaming others: the bachur who hits his finger and blames the hammer, the bachur who does not learn and blames the Rebbe and the classroom. This rationalization comes from gaavah, and it is why a Jewish apikorus, a child of the Avos, says he does not believe: he wants to follow his desires. He adds a joke about a man falling down the stairs and a philosopher's essay that there was never a true atheist.

title.en: The Six Day War and the letter about the beach

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the danger before the Six Day War and the open miracles in it, such as a burning house whose fire was put out when a second bomb burst the water tank on the roof. He tells of a woman who wrote to a newspaper asking it to stop writing about the miracles, because they disturbed her driving to the beach on Shabbos; this, he concludes, is the Jewish apikorus, who believes but says 'sour grapes'.

oneLiner.en: Through a chain of stories about Chassidic and Lithuanian gedolim, the Mashgiach shows how far tzaddikim went to guard another Jew's honor and never to shame him.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling that this year's talks to the bachurim have dealt with kavod chaveirim, honoring one's fellow, a weak point in the generation before Moshiach, when the Gemara says chutzpah will increase. Instead of direct mussar he tells stories of tzaddikim, since tzaddikim said such stories strengthen emunah. He then tells a series of maasios: the Chiddushei HaRim refusing to count in a minyan a man who had slapped another Jew, and warning against calling someone by a nickname; the Divrei Chaim making his son-in-law pay for a whole wedding after shaming a poor man; Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan keeping a poor man's secret; the Dukla Rav eating a pot of kerosene-tainted cholent to protect a maid; the refinement of Kelm; Rabbi Shmuel Salant's answer to a simple woman and his rebuke of a proud baal tokea; how Rabbi Yisrael Salanter's concern for a wagon driver won over the future founder of Novardok; and the Chofetz Chaim expelling a chutzpadik bachur while keeping a thief, based on the Mishnah in Avos.

en: The Mashgiach explains that in the time before Moshiach emunah is weak, and tzaddikim said that telling stories of tzaddikim strengthens it; therefore he tells stories rather than direct mussar.
Tzaddikim took extreme care not to come even into a doubt of shaming another Jew, as in the stories of Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan and the Divrei Chaim.
Working on mussar and kavod habriyos refines a person until he notices even fine points, like the smell of an extinguished havdalah candle bothering someone.
Rabbi Shmuel Salant taught that one may not embarrass anyone, especially someone who asks a foolish question, lest she be afraid to ask again.
Rabbi Yisrael Salanter interrupted an important mussar conversation so that a wagon driver would not be distressed, and seeing this made Rabbi Yosef Yoizel leave his business and become his talmid.
The Chofetz Chaim kept a bachur who stole but expelled one who spoke with chutzpah, because an az panim is presumed not to do teshuvah.

title.en: Honoring others and stories of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Mashgiach says this year's talks deal with kavod chaveirim, since chutzpah is a great test before Moshiach. He explains why he tells stories of tzaddikim instead of direct mussar: tzaddikim said such stories strengthen emunah, which will be very weak before Moshiach.

title.en: The Chiddushei HaRim's minyan and the nickname

summary.en: On his yahrzeit the Chiddushei HaRim wanted a small minyan; when a man forced his way in by slapping another Jew, the Rebbe refused to count him, citing Choshen Mishpat. He also warns a man who called a rav by a nickname, answering that Gehinom has room for everyone.

title.en: The Divrei Chaim and Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan

summary.en: The Divrei Chaim makes his son-in-law, who shamed a poor man collecting for his daughter's wedding, raise money for the whole wedding. Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan refuses to reveal the name of a ruined rich man even for a large donation, and the wealthy donor then reveals that he too is secretly poor.

title.en: The Dukla Rav's cholent and the refinement of Kelm

summary.en: Rabbi Avigdor Halberstam eats an entire pot of cholent tainted with kerosene so the host will not be angry at the maid. In Kelm, as Rabbi Yaakov Kamenetsky told, a forgotten yarmulke lay untouched for months, and the havdalah candle was put out outdoors so its smell would bother no one.

title.en: Rabbi Shmuel Salant: the cat and the shofar

summary.en: Rabbi Shmuel Salant answers a simple woman's foolish question about a cat with full seriousness so she will not be shamed. Then a young substitute baal tokea fails in the middle of the tekios, and Rabbi Shmuel tells him it was because he thought himself better than the old baal tokea.

title.en: Rabbi Yisrael Salanter and the Novardoker

summary.en: Rabbi Yosef Yoizel, a wealthy merchant, sees Rabbi Yisrael Salanter break off a mussar talk so a wagon driver would not be distressed, and leaves business to become his talmid and found the Novardok yeshivos. Later Rabbi Yoizel rebukes a man who shamed another and claimed it was worth losing Olam Haba.

title.en: Rabbi Elya Lopian and the Chofetz Chaim's ruling

summary.en: Rabbi Elya Lopian's wife is healed by a stranger he understood to be Eliyahu HaNavi, and the Sfas Emes knew of it. Rabbi Elya then relates, from the Chofetz Chaim's son-in-law, that the Chofetz Chaim kept a thief in yeshiva but expelled a bachur who spoke with chutzpah, explaining it from the Mishnah 'az panim l'Gehinom'.

oneLiner.en: Opening Tanya chapter 18, the Mashgiach explains the 'short way' for small minds: the hidden love and emunah every Jew inherits from the Avos, rooted in the chochmah at the core of the soul that is bound to the Or Ein Sof.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach first completes the previous chapter: a ba'al teshuvah, having sunk into the depths of tumah, raises sparks of kedushah no tzaddik can reach, and he illustrates it with the story of the Bach in Gehinnom. Turning to chapter 18, he reviews the 'long way' of contemplation through chochmah and binah and introduces the 'short way' for small souls who cannot dwell on Hashem's greatness. Every Jew has a hidden love and natural emunah, an inheritance from the Avos, who are true fathers. A Jew who denies Hashem is like a sick stomach that has lost its appetite. The Avos were a merkavah for Hashem and passed this to all their descendants, down to the lowest soul, whose inner core is chochmah, bound to the Or Ein Sof, because souls are not created yesh me'ayin. From the Sefer HaGilgulim he explains how a rasha can beget a tzaddik, and how Moshiach's lineage was hidden in klippah from the Satan.

en: Tanya chapter 18 begins a 'short way' for people whose minds cannot dwell long on Hashem's greatness, after the 'long way' of chochmah and binah in the earlier chapters.
Every Jew has a hidden love and a natural emunah in Hashem, an inheritance from the Avos rather than something acquired.
Because the Avos were a merkavah for Hashem, they passed His powers on to all their descendants, even to the lowest soul of nefesh de'nefesh of Malchus de'Asiyah.
Hidden in every soul is chochmah, its inner core, in which the Or Ein Sof is clothed.
Jewish souls, unlike the rest of creation, are not made yesh me'ayin but are a direct extension from Hashem, like children.
Since even a rasha's inner core is bound to the Ein Sof, a rasha can sometimes beget a tzaddik far greater than himself.

title.en: The ba'al teshuvah raises lost sparks

summary.en: Completing the previous chapter, the Mashgiach explains that sparks of kedushah scattered by Adam's sin are raised when used for good, that the higher the kedushah the deeper it sank, and that a rasha who does teshuvah lifts sparks no tzaddik can reach.

title.en: The Bach in Gehinnom

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Bach, found without sin, had to pass briefly through Gehinnom because a sneeze moved a wagon drawn by an ox and a horse, and there he decreed that its fire be put out for forty days, raising the resha'im with him.

title.en: From the long way to the short way

summary.en: Opening chapter 18, the Mashgiach reviews the earlier chapters: love and fear born of chochmah and binah, or at least a mind that understands. He then introduces the chapters for small souls who cannot harness their minds, and the Tanya's reminder that one would give his life rather than serve avodah zarah, as the 'short way' promised on the title page.

title.en: 'Very near': a third way

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of chapter 18 on the passuk 'very near to you': even one who cannot meditate on Hashem's greatness nor understand it with his mind has a third way, emunah, and the love in his heart is real, not imagined.

title.en: An inheritance from the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the hidden love is an inheritance from the Avos, called fathers and not grandfathers because their closeness never fades. Every Jew believes; one who denies is like a man who spoiled his stomach and lost his appetite, while the craving is still there.

title.en: The Avos as a merkavah

summary.en: Asking what the root of this love is, the Mashgiach explains that the Avos were a merkavah for Hashem, like the chariot Yechezkel saw, never separated from Him for a moment, and so they passed all the G-dly powers of the ten sefiros to every descendant, even to the poshei Yisrael.

title.en: Chochmah at the core of every soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the levels of souls, from Atzilus down to nefesh de'nefesh of Malchus de'Asiyah, and explains that since the sefiros are bound into one, even the lowest soul contains chochmah, its inner kernel, in which the Or Ein Sof rests, as the pesukim say Hashem founded the world with chochmah.

title.en: Not yesh me'ayin but a direct extension

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that all creation comes from Hashem as beriah, something from nothing, but a Jewish soul is a direct extension from Him, like a child. Like life that fills every limb of the body, this G-dly chochmah gives life to every Jew, high or low.

title.en: A rasha who begets a tzaddik

summary.en: From the Arizal's Sefer HaGilgulim the Mashgiach asks how a rasha can beget a tzaddik if each creature begets its own kind, and answers that the rasha's inner core is bound to the Ein Sof. He then explains that Yaakov and Esav were born together so that the Samach Mem would have no complaint about the balance of good and evil.

title.en: Two kinds of admoni

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Esav the admoni, a shedder of blood drawn to red, with David, an admoni with beautiful eyes whose bloodshed was with the Sanhedrin's permission, and mentions the custom not to wear red. He then brings the Midrash that the Satan guarded against Moshiach's birth, and so it came hidden, as with Moav, whom the Satan never suspected.

title.en: Great souls hidden in klippah

summary.en: The Mashgiach continues with Rus and David, whom the Satan took for his own, and with the Arizal's account of Avraham's birth, concluding that a rasha can draw down a holy soul hidden in klippah because even he holds chochmah bound to the Ein Sof. Answering a question at the end, he distinguishes a middah, which habit can change, from an existing entity such as the love of Hashem in every Jew.

oneLiner.en: Speaking at the resting place of Shimon HaTzaddik as a new zman of learning begins, the Mashgiach explains how place, time and soul come together in a time of Divine favor, and calls for early prayer and strengthened yiras Shamayim in a dangerous time.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a l'chaim and a prayer at the resting place of Shimon HaTzaddik. Using the threefold division of olam, shanah and nefesh (place, time and soul), he notes that parshas Re'eh introduces 'the place Hashem will choose', while the coming forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul are a time of favor that Moshe Rabbeinu's prayer established. Shimon HaTzaddik is the 'soul' of favor: Rav Yehoshua Leib Diskin sent people to pray there, and in time of war a Rebbe sent people there rather than only to the Kosel. He began the toil and chiddushim of the Oral Torah and is the first named in Pirkei Avos, so it is a fitting place to pray for success at the start of a new zman. The Mashgiach then ties this week's middah of tiferes to Torah through the haftarah, counts the mentions of 'the chosen place' and of simchah in the parsha, and turns to the dangers facing Jews, urging prayer before trouble and strength against today's trials, citing the Akeidah. He closes with the hillula of the Satmar Rav and a story of his ruach hakodesh.

en: Every matter exists in place, time and soul; parshas Re'eh reveals a 'place of favor', Elul is a 'time of favor', and Shimon HaTzaddik is the 'soul' through which favor comes.
The novelty of Moshe Rabbeinu's last forty days is that after the sin of the Golden Calf a time of favor came into being, from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, established through his prayer.
The toil, pilpul and chiddushim of the Oral Torah began with Shimon HaTzaddik, which is why tzaddikim called his resting place the cradle of the Oral Torah.
One must pray before trouble arrives, because once harsh judgment rules it is harder for prayer to be accepted.
Hashem placed this generation among great trials in tznius, guarding the eyes and guarding thought, and withstanding them through yiras Shamayim is its task.

title.en: Place, time and soul of favor

summary.en: After a l'chaim and a prayer at the resting place of Shimon HaTzaddik, the Mashgiach applies the division of olam, shanah and nefesh: parshas Re'eh reveals 'the place Hashem will choose', and the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur became a time of favor after the sin of the Golden Calf.

title.en: Shimon HaTzaddik, cradle of the Oral Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a time of favor needs prayer, and that Shimon HaTzaddik's resting place is a place of favor because of his soul. He tells how Rav Yehoshua Leib Diskin sent people to pray there and how in wartime a Rebbe sent people there, and explains that the Oral Torah's pilpul began with Shimon HaTzaddik, the first named in Pirkei Avos, so it is the place to pray for success in the new zman.

title.en: Tiferes, simchah and the dangers of the hour

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the third week of consolation to the middah of tiferes, which is Torah, through the haftarah, and notes that 'the place Hashem will choose' and simchah recur many times in the parsha. He then describes the dangers facing Jews: attacks this week, the passing of three great Torah sages, and the threatened move for a state at the UN, and calls to pray that no Jew be harmed.

title.en: Prayer before trouble; trials of this generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one should pray before trouble comes, since once judgment rules prayer is harder to accept, and urges asking now for a new year of renewal and yiras Shamayim. He describes today's trials in tznius and guarding eyes and thoughts as this generation's task, and brings the Akeidah, where Avraham's trial revealed his fear of G-d.

title.en: The Satmar Rav's hillula and a story

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks for prayer that all of Klal Yisrael withstand the trials before Moshiach, mentions that the hillula of the Satmar Rav falls that night and praises how he saved Jews for Torah, and after a l'chaim tells how the Satmar Rav once detained a businessman for two hours, saving him from men waiting at his shop.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim, the Mashgiach traces how the Ba'al Shem Tov revived the broken masses, warns against Chassidus turned into team rivalry and politics, and explains through the Yesod HaAvodah's parable of grass that grows by the moon that every Jew grows through the rebbe and chevra of his own soul-root.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the decline of the Jewish masses after the gezeiros of Tach v'Tat, when the common people fell to a very low level. The Ba'al Shem Tov was sent to strengthen them with simple emunah, and where Chassidus did not reach, above all in Germany, Haskalah and Reform took hold; the Meshech Chochmah wrote that the destruction would begin there. He tells how the Satan, unable to stop Chassidus, threatened to make his own chassidim, and sees this in Chassidus turned into a team rivalry. Turning to the bachurim, he urges constant self-strengthening, sincere learning and davening with kavanah, and says his material comes from sefarim and his rebbes. Through the shevatim, the Yesod HaAvodah's parable of grass growing by the moon, and the Haflaah's teaching that a talmid is destined for his rebbe like a shidduch, he explains that each Jew grows through his own root, and closes with the purpose of their weekly gatherings.

en: After the gezeiros of Tach v'Tat the masses fell low, and the Ba'al Shem Tov came to raise them with simple emunah, tefillah and joy.
Where Chassidus did not take root, above all in Germany, Haskalah and Reform spread, and from there the destruction began.
Chassidus that becomes rivalry between rebbes, like sports teams, with politics and quarrels, is not true Chassidus; one should seek a rebbe who serves Hashem without politics.
Like the shevatim, each with its own gate, nusach and nasi yet all bound to Yaakov Avinu, every Jew belongs to a soul-root and grows through the rebbe of that root.
A talmid's rebbe and his chevra are arranged from Heaven like a shidduch, and the purpose of the gatherings is that all become better ovdei Hashem.

title.en: The decline after Tach v'Tat

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the generations grew smaller through the galus, and how after the gezeiros of Tach v'Tat the common people were broken and fell to a very low level in yiras Shamayim, even while great gedolim still lived.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and Germany

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Ba'al Shem Tov was sent to strengthen the masses with simple emunah, while Germany, where Chassidus never entered, fell to Haskalah and Reform. He tells how the Satan threatened to make his own chassidim, so the Ba'al Shem Tov did not send talmidim there, and cites the Meshech Chochmah that the destruction would begin in Germany.

title.en: Chassidus like a sports team

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how generations of tzaddikim spread serving Hashem with joy and good davening, and then laments that politics and machlokes crept into Chassidus, so that people treat their rebbe like a baseball team. He says one should seek a rebbe who serves Hashem without politics and does not speak against other rebbes.

title.en: What a bachur must want

summary.en: Addressing the bachurim, the Mashgiach says one must constantly strengthen oneself and ask for whom one learns, want to become a talmid chacham with sincerity and not for honor, and pray to Hashem with pesukim of Tehillim. He describes the weekly gatherings and stresses davening with kavanah, learning before davening, and friends strengthening each other.

title.en: Speaking from the sefarim

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the principle of tzaddikim that a rebbe who teaches avodas Hashem must himself live by it, and answers that he may speak because his material comes from sefarim and from what he saw by his rebbes. He tells how sefarim gave him life, and that he drew from Chassidish and Litvish sefarim and from many rebbes, not attaching to only one path.

title.en: Shevatim, roots and rebbes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sanzer Rav's rebuke of a chassid who called his own rebbe the greatest and the others worthless. He explains that after the seven shepherds came the shevatim, each with its own gate in the Beis HaMikdash, nusach and nasi, all bound to Yaakov Avinu, and that every Jew grows from the rebbe of his own soul-root.

title.en: The Yesod HaAvodah and his chassid

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Yesod HaAvodah met a chassid who had stopped coming and asked him for the truth without politics; the chassid said he goes to Reb Aharon of Karlin, a greater rebbe. The Yesod HaAvodah agreed, and began his answer with the teaching that every blade of grass has an angel that strikes it and says grow, and with Rashi on the blessing of Yosef that some crops grow by the sun and some by the moon.

title.en: Grass of the moon; a rebbe like a shidduch

summary.en: The Mashgiach completes the parable: grass that grows by the moon and wants the sun is struck and told it will only burn there, so the chassid would grow by the Yesod HaAvodah. He brings the Haflaah that just as a bas kol announces a match before a child is formed, it announces which rebbe a talmid belongs to, compares it to finding one's single zivug among millions, and says Hashem arranges by hashgacha pratis that each chaburah gathers together.

title.en: The purpose of the gatherings

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the gatherings are to give eitzos for coming close to Hashem, without politics, as a holy chevra and not a team. Their purpose is that all become better ovdei Hashem, and he closes with brachos that the gatherings bring nachas ruach to Hashem.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem is hidden in the world and is found only through reflection, while Yidden can see Him plainly in the Torah, and he shows this through two examples: the share of Shevet Levi among the teachers of Torah, and the endless depth of the Torah itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that the word olam (world) comes from he'elem, hiddenness: Hashem runs every detail of creation, yet one sees Him only by reflecting, which is why heretics claim the world made itself. Yidden, he says, can see the Ribono shel Olam plainly in the Torah, and he gives two examples. First, Moshe blessed Shevet Levi that they would teach the Torah's laws to Yisrael, and one sees it: most roshei yeshiva in Torah Vodaath and most of the great commentators on the Shulchan Aruch were kohanim or levi'im, though the Rambam teaches that anyone can rise to that holiness. Second, the Torah has no end: a child and an old gadol learn the same Chumash and the same Bava Metzia and keep finding new things, because it was given with prophecy and ruach hakodesh, unlike a professor's textbooks. He ends with a story of a frum scientist who exposed the falsehood of the heretical scientists.

en: The world is called olam because Hashem's guidance is hidden in it; only one who reflects comes to see that there is a Ribono shel Olam.
Yidden can see the Ribono shel Olam plainly in the Torah and in Yiddishkeit, as through a small opening in the blanket that covers the world.
Moshe's blessing that Levi would teach the Torah's laws to Yaakov is visible in practice: a disproportionate share of roshei yeshiva and of the great poskim and commentators were kohanim and levi'im.
Following the Rambam, a Jew who is not a Levi can also dedicate himself to Torah and become a great talmid chacham; for a Levi it is only easier.
The Torah has no end: the same Chumash and the same Gemara serve a person from childhood to old age, and each time he sees new things in them.
This is because the Torah was given through prophecy and the Gemara with ruach hakodesh; the Ribono shel Olam is eternal and so is His Torah, unlike the books of any professor.

title.en: Olam means hidden

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that olam comes from the word for hidden, brings the Reishis Chochmah that the world itself, not Gehinom, is what is out in the street, and describes how Hashem's hidden guidance lets heretics claim the world made itself. With the parable of a rich heretic's house he shows that reflection reveals the Ribono shel Olam.

title.en: Shevet Levi as teachers of Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Yidden see Hashem plainly in the Torah and gives the first example: Moshe's blessing that Levi teach the Torah's laws. He notes that of ten roshei yeshiva in Torah Vodaath seven were kohanim or levi'im, and goes through the commentators around the Shulchan Aruch, most of them kohanim or levi'im.

title.en: Concise halachah seforim and malchus

summary.en: As the generations weakened, concise halachah seforim were written: the Mishnah Berurah, the Aruch HaShulchan and the Shulchan Aruch HaRav, whose authors were Yisraelim. The Mashgiach explains that the Chassidishe Rebbes and the Ba'al HaTanya, descended from David HaMelech, represent malchus, a different aspect from the teachers of Levi.

title.en: The Brisker derech and the Rambam

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the derech of Reb Chaim Brisker spread as the generations weakened, and that his leading talmidim included kohanim; in his own beis medrash the kohanim are disproportionately many. He then brings the Rambam that any Jew who devotes himself to Torah becomes holy like the kohanim and levi'im, so a non-Levi can also become a great talmid chacham.

title.en: The same Chumash for a lifetime

summary.en: The second example: a child in secular school replaces his books every term, but a Jewish child learns the same Chumash at five and at eighty, and the same Bava Metzia at eight and as a gadol, as the Chasam Sofer, the Gra, the Rambam and the Rosh did. The Mashgiach explains that this is because the Torah was given through prophecy and the Gemara with ruach hakodesh, and Hashem's Torah is eternal.

title.en: New chiddushim every year; the scientists

summary.en: A professor understands his textbook at once and needs a new book for new things, but a talmid chacham sees new things in the same Gemara every year, which the Mashgiach ties to the passuk that Hashem gave His laws only to Yisrael. Great Rebbes wrote a new kuntres on the sedra each year, as the Chasam Sofer and Sfas Emes show. He adds that the goyim will be punished for not recognizing the Creator, and that scientists are no more heretical than a baker, only given a microphone.

title.en: The frum head of the atomic commission

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how, about forty years earlier, the frum Jew who headed the Federal Atomic Energy Commission spoke in his yeshiva and exposed the falsehood of the heretical scientists. He concludes that a goy must reach Hashem through reflection while Yidden see Him, as the two examples of Shevet Levi and the Torah's depth show.

catalogTitle: טבע נשמות ישראל להיות בטל להקב"ה לגמרי י"ט כדי להתאחד באור אין סוף ב"ה וב"ש.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Tanya chapter 18: because Hashem is clothed in the Chochmah of every Jewish soul, even the simplest Jew has an instinctive emunah, above reason, that makes him ready to give his life rather than deny Hashem's unity.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling the levels of the previous chapter and asks how the verse 'it is very close to you' applies to a Jew who cannot even intellectually grasp Hashem's greatness. The answer begins with the Avos, whose qualities their children inherit. He then explains Chochmah as the fountain of intellect: the sudden spark, above the mind, that Binah develops, compared to the tefillin above the brain. Since no thought can grasp Hashem, emunah is above reason, like a child's knowledge of his parents. He brings the Chasam Sofer's ruling that a son may not kill his father who breaks in, because a father's bond to his son is instinctive. With 'a simple one believes everything', 'I was like a beast with You' and 'an ox knows its owner', he shows that this emunah is instinct. Hence even the lowest Jews gave their lives, unlike drilled soldiers, and nearly all keep milah and avoid chametz.

en: Chochmah is the source of intellect: a spark from above that the mind receives but cannot grasp, which Binah then develops into understanding.
Emunah is above reason; in emunah everyone is like a simple fool, and the greatest wisdom in emunah is simple faith.
A Jew knows Hashem by intuition, the way a child knows his father and mother without being able to explain why.
Even the lowest Jews gave their lives rather than deny Hashem's unity, not out of thought or drilling, but by an instinct like a mother animal protecting its young.
Idolatry is like suicide for the neshamah, so a Jew instinctively gives up his body to save it, as a hand reflexively shields the eye.

candidateTopics: Chasam Sofer on a father who breaks in

title.en: The third level and the legacy of the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the levels of the previous chapter and asks how the verse 'it is very close to you' applies to a Jew who cannot even intellectually grasp Hashem's greatness. He explains that the Avos were a merkavah, and their children inherit their qualities, revealed or hidden.

title.en: Chochmah, the fountain of intellect

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chochmah is not wisdom but the source of the sudden spark of insight that Binah develops. He compares it to tefillin, which sit above the brain, brings Pasach Eliyahu, and reads Chochmah as 'koach mah', a power we cannot grasp.

title.en: Pure logic and emunah above reason

summary.en: The Mashgiach says no thought can grasp Hashem, discusses the Gemara that women have extra Binah yet rarely pure logic, and adds that most men's thinking is also biased by desire. Emunah is above reason, like a child who knows his parents without understanding why.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer on a father and son

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer's ruling that a son may not kill his father who breaks in, even if the father does not recognize him, because a father instinctively will not kill his son. With Reb Chaim Brisker's remark on the Rosh, he explains that a ruling without proof comes from a mind molded by Torah.

title.en: The simple one, the beast and the ox

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'a simple one believes everything' and says the greatest wisdom in emunah is simplicity. He explains 'I was like a beast with You' and 'an ox knows its owner': an animal knows its master by instinct, and so does a Jew.

title.en: Self-sacrifice by instinct, not by thought

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even the lowest Jews endure torture rather than deny Hashem without thinking it through, like a mother animal defending its young. He contrasts this with soldiers who were trained to give their lives for the king.

title.en: The chassid and the flogged soldier

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a chassid who came to the Ba'al HaTanya after years away; he had seen a soldier flogged for coming back from guard duty with frozen ears, and that stirred his davening for years. He explains that today there is no fear of the king, and describes how soldiers were drilled until they would die for the king.

title.en: Undrilled Jews who gave their lives

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that no Jew would blow himself up for a political leader, yet history shows sinful Jews who let themselves be killed in the Crusades rather than convert. He adds that one who says Shema with intent and readies himself for mesirus nefesh, as the Zohar says, has worked himself up to it.

title.en: Exceptions, and milah and chametz

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tzemach Tzedek that sins connected with gentiles, such as chalav akum, yayin nesech or chametz on Pesach, deaden the feeling for mesirus nefesh. He mentions a survey in Eretz Yisrael that nearly everyone keeps milah and avoids chametz, and explains that Hashem Echad lights up the whole soul through Chochmah.

title.en: Milah above reason; idolatry as suicide of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the dispute of Yishmael and Yitzchak over milah and explains that milah is above daas, in a Jew's blood. Idolatry is suicide for the neshamah, so a Jew instinctively sacrifices the body for it, like a hand shielding the eye; he closes with a remark on Greek culture.

oneLiner.en: On the eve of 21 Kislev the Mashgiach tells the bachurim how Hashem saved the Satmar Rav from Hungary to rebuild Yiddishkeit in America, and tells a public miracle of the Stoliner Rebbe, whose yahrzeit is the same day.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by telling the bachurim that their coming voluntarily, with no tests or marks, in a generation of an unprecedented yetzer hara, is itself a wonder, as tzaddikim foretold that before Moshiach Hashem would help Jewish children learn Torah. Tonight and tomorrow, 21 Kislev, are an eis ratzon for davening and learning. He then tells how the Satmar Rav, the great opponent of the Zionists, was saved from Hungary on the Kasztner train after Kasztner's late mother warned him in a dream that the whole train depended on it. Describing pre-war America, where Jews lost their children for lack of rabbanim and kashrus, he applies Yosef's words that he was sent ahead for sustenance: the Satmar Rav was saved to rebuild Yiddishkeit in America. He adds the yahrzeit of the Stoliner Rebbe and tells a public miracle about a tenant's eviction case, then closes with requests for warm lechaim and a refuah.

en: Bachurim coming to learn of their own will, with nobody forcing them, in this generation of a mighty yetzer hara, is a wonder that tzaddikim foretold for the time before Moshiach.
Tonight and tomorrow, 21 Kislev, are a great eis ratzon, and the Mashgiach says that knowing this should arouse one in davening and learning, since tefillah is then easily accepted.
Heaven arranged that the Zionist Kasztner, warned in a dream by his late mother, took the Satmar Rav onto his train, and in the Mashgiach's merit the whole train was saved.
Like Yosef, sent ahead 'for sustenance', the Satmar Rav was saved in order to rebuild Yiddishkeit in America, where before the war it had been almost lost.
The Stoliner Rebbe was a ba'al mofes, and his promise that an eviction case would be thrown out came true before the eyes of everyone in the court.

candidateTopics: the Satmar Rav's rescue from Hungary

title.en: Bachurim who come freely, and the eis ratzon

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the bachurim that nobody forces them to come and they get no tests or marks, so their coming in this generation of an unprecedented yetzer hara is a wonder that tzaddikim foretold. He adds that tonight and tomorrow, 21 Kislev, are an eis ratzon in which davening is easily accepted.

title.en: The Satmar Rav and the Kasztner train

summary.en: The Mashgiach recounts the destruction of Hungarian Jewry and the Satmar Rav's fight against the Zionists. Kasztner, a Zionist leader, arranged a train out of Hungary for Zionists and refused the Satmar chassidim's money, until his late mother warned him in a dream that the whole train depended on saving the Satmar Rav.

title.en: Sent ahead to rebuild Yiddishkeit in America

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes pre-war America, where only two or three of over a hundred chassidish Jews in his father's shtibel kept their children shomrei Shabbos, for lack of rabbanim and kashrus. He applies Yosef's words 'lemichya shelachani' to the Satmar Rav, who grew from thirty at his tish to tens of thousands, and finishes the rescue story: the train was saved in his merit, and 21 Kislev became a day of thanksgiving.

title.en: The Stoliner Rebbe's yahrzeit

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the day is also the yahrzeit of R' Yochanan, the Stoliner Rebbe, who was saved miraculously and came to America, and describes his davening and his constant mofsim. He chooses one story because it happened in public, and sets it up: a Stoliner chassid, a singer, got a hard-to-find apartment near the shul on condition that he put out the garbage cans.

title.en: The eviction case thrown out

summary.en: Because of rent control, the landlady sued to evict the chassid when he once left the garbage over Pesach. The Stoliner Rebbe foretold each postponement, and on the last possible date, erev Rosh Hashanah, he said the case would be thrown out; in the middle of the hearing a telegram called the judge home and he dismissed the case. The Mashgiach recalls how the Stoliner Rebbe and his chassidim davened warmly.

title.en: Lechaim, a request for a refuah, and farewell

summary.en: In closing, the Mashgiach asks the bachurim for a warm lechaim and says he is sure it will help him toward a refuah. He tells them he will not come in the coming weeks because of his doctors' treatment, and blesses them with a joyous Shabbos and a bright Chanukah.

oneLiner.en: At Kever Rochel on the last day of Av, the Mashgiach explains that Elul is a month Yaakov 'grabbed' from Esav, that Rachel's son Binyamin carries the power to grab back what is truly Klal Yisrael's, and that today one must grab oneself out of the yetzer hara through Torah together with tefillah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach speaks at Kever Rochel as Av ends. He cites the Zohar that the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav, and that Yaakov grabbed Elul (and Mordechai grabbed Adar). A Midrash tells of a maiden who, in the generation of the Nefilim, seized an angel's wings, flew to the Throne of Glory and became the mazal Besulah, the mazal of Elul; since a mazal is a flow of influence, Elul's influence is the power to grab oneself free. He then turns to Rachel: Binyamin, born as she died, is her essence, and in the merit of her self-giving, described in the Midrash of her plea after the Churban, Binyamin can grab back what Esav holds, as on Tu B'Av in Shiloh. He applies this to resolutions for Elul, to today's electronic yetzer hara, to Torah and tefillah as inseparable, with a story of the Atzei Chaim, and closes with the tefillah of Rebbe Reb Elimelech.

en: According to the Zohar the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav, and Yaakov grabbed the month of Elul from Esav's portion.
A mazal is a flow of influence onto its month; Elul's mazal, Besulah, came from a maiden who grabbed an angel's wings, so Elul's influence is the power to grab.
Binyamin, born as Rachel died, is the essence of his mother, and he carries the merit of her giving away her portion.
Through Binyamin, Tu B'Av became a day of grabbing, when the men of Binyamin took wives in Shiloh.
At the start of Elul one must take resolutions and grab oneself free of the yetzer hara, which today has trapped even fine young men through electronics.
Torah and tefillah must go together: one cannot have tefillah without Torah nor merit Torah without tefillah, and this is the only advice for staying holy today.

title.en: Elul, the month Yaakov grabbed

summary.en: Speaking at the place of Rachel Imeinu, the Mashgiach brings the Zohar that the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav, and that Yaakov went and grabbed Elul, as Mordechai grabbed Adar.

title.en: The maiden who became mazal Besulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash of the maiden who grabbed an angel's wings and was set as the mazal of Elul, explains that a mazal is a flow of influence, and says Elul's influence is the strength to grab oneself out of the sitra achra.

title.en: Rachel's self-giving and Binyamin

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Binyamin, born as Rachel died, is her essence, retells the Midrash of Rachel's plea after the Churban, when she gave up her portion so as not to shame her sister, and concludes that Binyamin has the merit to take back what Esav wants to keep.

title.en: Binyamin grabs: Tu B'Av and Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Esav's hold on the months is only external, since the whole creation is for Yisrael, then brings the account in Shoftim of Binyamin's men grabbing wives in Shiloh and the Gemara in Taanis on Tu B'Av, and shows how Binyamin grabbed part of Av at Tu B'Av and part of Teves at Chanukah.

title.en: Resolutions at Kever Rochel as Av ends

summary.en: Sitting at Rachel's grave on the last day of Av, the Mashgiach calls for resolutions not to let oneself be held by the yetzer hara, and describes how, as a mashgiach, he sees fine young men trapped by the electronic yetzer hara of today, who need real mesirus nefesh to break free.

title.en: Torah and tefillah together

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that tefillah cannot exist without Torah nor Torah without tefillah, tells of a young man who came to the Atzei Chaim about foreign thoughts, and says that Hashem has sent every Jew on a shlichus in this world where Torah with tefillah is the only way to stay holy; he calls on all to grab this advice as Elul begins.

title.en: The tefillah of Rebbe Reb Elimelech

summary.en: After recalling the earnest davening of figures he remembers, the Mashgiach speaks of the nations' plans for a state at the UN and says that Hashem runs the world, yet we need protection; Rebbe Reb Elimelech nullified the birth pangs of Moshiach, and he urges saying his tefillah before davening.

catalogTitle: האדם צריך לעשות חשבון שהרי כדי שלא לעבוד ע"ז הי' מוסר נפשו' וכל עבירה הוי מרידה בהקב"ה והוי ממש כמו ע"ז.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's image of the soul as 'the candle of Hashem': like a flame that surges upward to its source even at the cost of its own existence, the Jewish soul by nature longs to be nullified in Hashem, the way of kedushah, while tumah clings to its own ego.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by recalling the previous chapter: even simple Jews steeped in sin are ready to give their lives rather than serve idols, and the coming chapters explain why. He introduces the verse 'the soul of man is the candle of Hashem', and expands with a thought on Chanukah as a glimpse of the light of Moshiach, illustrated by a story of the Chozeh of Lublin. Returning to the Tanya, he describes how a flame surges upward to rejoin its root in the sphere of the moon, why it flickers from side to side, and why Jews sway when they learn. Unlike every other being, fire is ready to be extinguished to return to its source; the soul likewise longs to be nullified in Hashem. He explains that 'nature' means what reason cannot explain, then contrasts kedushah, rooted in Chochmah and bittul, with tumah, which is ego. This leads to true humility, the selfish 'giver' of kelipah called Kna'ani, and the tzaddik whose body alone holds his soul back.

en: The soul is 'the candle of Hashem': like a flame, which always surges upward to rejoin its root, the soul by nature longs to leave and cleave to its source, Hashem.
Fire is the exception in creation: every other being fights to preserve its existence, yet fire is ready to be extinguished as long as it returns to its root, and the soul is the same.
The word 'nature' is a borrowed term for whatever cannot be explained by reason; the soul's urge to cleave to Hashem is 'nature' in this sense, higher than logic, because it comes from Chochmah.
Kedushah means bittul, being ready to be nullified to Hashem, while tumah is ego: it insists on its own separate existence.
True humility is not feeling inferior but having no sense of self apart from Hashem; such an anav is always joyful, while one who is depressed over his shortcomings is really showing pride.
In kedushah the giving side is stronger than the receiving side; in the sitra achra the 'giver' really gives for himself, and that is why it is called Kna'ani, from the word for submitting.
The tzaddik surges toward Hashem without concern for his own existence; only his body, the 'wick', holds his soul back until his time comes.

title.en: Why sinners give their lives; the candle of Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that even sinners are ready for mesiras nefesh against idolatry and says the coming chapters explain why. He introduces 'the soul of man is the candle of Hashem' and brings the teaching that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos are fit for Chanukah, applied to souls that Shabbos does not ignite but Chanukah does.

title.en: Chanukah, light of Moshiach, and the Chozeh's story

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chanukah's eight lights reach beyond Shabbos's seven into the light of Moshiach, so it can stir even distant souls; when a Jew lights below, Hashem lights his soul above. He tells the story of the Chozeh of Lublin, who would not curse an informer at the moment he was lighting Chanukah candles.

title.en: Why a flame surges upward

summary.en: Back in the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that a flame always stands upright because it wants to tear loose from the wick and rejoin the general element of fire, whose root is in the sphere of the moon. He describes the invisible spheres and the Rambam's statement that they are pure like clear glass, and the rule that every being yearns for its origin.

title.en: Bedikas chametz at night; why Jews sway

summary.en: The Mashgiach uses the flame's root in the moon to explain why a candle works better at night, hence bedikas chametz at night. The flame shakes side to side like a tooth being pulled, and so Jews sway when they learn or daven; he tells of two babies mixed up at birth, where the one who swayed over Gemara was the Jew.

title.en: Fire and soul ready for self-nullification

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the flame strives to free itself even though it would then be extinguished, against the rule that every being fights to preserve itself. The soul, including its lower levels of ruach and nefesh, acts likewise: it longs to cleave to Hashem, the source of all life, even if it would cease to exist as itself.

title.en: What 'nature' means: beyond explanation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the word 'nature' is a borrowed term for what has no reason. He brings the Rashab's point that a scientist can say a hard, sharp knife cuts soft challah but not why, and the example of a machine whose workings can be explained only down to a point; the soul's urge to cleave to Hashem is 'nature' in this sense.

title.en: Kedushah is bittul, tumah is ego; true humility

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chochmah is the potential that produces logic and is higher than it. In kedushah there is an urge to be nullified to Hashem, while tumah is ego, the 'capital I'. He then defines true humility as having no self apart from Hashem, shows how Dovid HaMelech could demand honor without ego, and says a true anav is always joyful.

title.en: Kelipah acts for itself; right over left

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that whoever draws from Chochmah is nullified and lacks nothing, while kelipah does everything for itself, even its mitzvos. He interprets Chochmah as 'koach mah', the power of nothingness, and lists the seven middos of kelipah, such as its self-praise. In kedushah the giving, right side of chesed dominates, as seen in tefillin, washing and dressing the right side first.

title.en: In kelipah the receiver rules: Kna'ani

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ohr HaChaim's account of his struggle with two dogs, male and female, where the female was far harder to overcome, because in the sitra achra the receiving side is stronger. He applies this to the nations' 'ladies first' and to Rashi's contrast of Yaakov and Esav, and explains that chesed of kelipah is called Kna'ani because its 'giver' really gives for himself.

title.en: The merchant, the tzaddik, and the word 'me'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why a merchant is called Kna'ani, then contrasts the tzaddik who gives out of pure chesed and surges to Hashem, held back only by his body, the wick. He brings Nadav and Avihu and Sarah Imeinu as souls that flew out from closeness to Hashem, and closes with a story of a son who learned nothing if he can still say 'me'.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach tells bachurim that a Jew must rise higher every day, that the day is built by going to sleep on time and waking with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim, and that every act of a Jew affects all of creation and other Jewish souls.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Avraham Avinu, who kept travelling higher, and with the Yid HaKadosh, for whom each day was a new level: a Jew cannot stand still, so each morning must begin fresh. The real preparation for the day is the night before: going to sleep on time, sleeping enough, and lying down with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim and Krias Shema al hamitah, as the opening of the Shulchan Aruch implies. On waking, the first thought, word and act belong to Hashem: Modeh Ani, negel vasser, no snooze button, since everything follows the beginning. He then explains that man is master of creation; in the generation of the Flood even the earth sinned through its owners, while Noach's portion was saved. Every Jew affects other souls of his root, so negel vasser purifies the whole world, and a Jew fighting the yetzer hara is fighting for others too. He ends with the Sanzer Rav and a bachur's excuses for coming late.

en: A Jew can never stand in one place like an angel; he either rises or falls, so each day must be better than the last.
The day really begins the night before: going to sleep on time, sleeping enough, and lying down with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim.
The first thought, the first word and the first act of the morning should be for Hashem, since the whole day follows its beginning.
Man is the master of creation; each Jew has a portion of the world, which is elevated or spoiled by his deeds.
Jews are bound to one another, so a mitzvah such as negel vasser purifies not only the one who does it but other souls of his root and all of creation.

title.en: Rising higher each day, and going to sleep on time

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Avraham's continual travelling higher and the Yid HaKadosh, for whom each day was a new level, and says a Jew cannot stand still like an angel. He then teaches that the day is prepared the night before: going to sleep on time without idle talk, and sleeping enough to be alert in the shiur.

title.en: Lying down with kabbalas ol malchus shamayim

summary.en: Through Rabbi Meir of Premishlan's reading of the first halacha of the Shulchan Aruch, the Mashgiach explains that one who goes to sleep like a lion rises like a lion. He speaks of Krias Shema al hamitah, which drives away harmful forces, and of the verse in Mishlei about the sluggard, read as a call to go to sleep on time.

title.en: The first thought, word and act of the morning

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes waking with kabbalas ol: Modeh Ani said aloud and with feeling, explained in two ways, and getting up at once without the snooze button. Like a bachur who jumps up early on the day he leaves for camp, a Jew should rise each day for avodas Hashem, dedicating his first thought, speech and deed.

title.en: Man as master of creation; the Flood

summary.en: From Tehillim, that all was placed under man's feet, the Mashgiach explains how in the generation of the Flood even animals and the earth sinned: each person's portion of creation is spoiled by his sins. Noach's portion, including Eretz Yisrael, did not sin and was spared.

title.en: Jews bound together like one body

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that some Jews, even simple ones with lofty souls, are leaders over hundreds, and that through man's conduct angels, sun and moon praise Hashem better. Like limbs of one body, where an infected finger sickens the whole body, Jews are intermixed, and a mitzvah lights up many souls of one's root, according to the level of one's soul.

title.en: A tzaddik's late candle-lighting; fighting for others

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a tzaddik who lit Shabbos candles slightly late and whose truthful student admitted it, and explains that Hashem may let a tzaddik stumble so that his teshuvah arouses others. Each Jew influences those of his root; his negel vasser purifies others too, and when fighting the yetzer hara he should remember that his sin harms other Jews.

title.en: The responsibility of a general

summary.en: The Mashgiach says negel vasser purifies not only the hands but the body and all of creation, and that being a Jew is a responsibility like that of a general whose mistake can lose a war. The first thought, word and deed of the morning are malchus shamayim, and every tefillah and mitzvah acts in the upper and lower worlds.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav and the excuse

summary.en: Speaking of a bachur who comes late with a good excuse, the Mashgiach tells of a man who came to the Sanzer Rav in a new bekishe of old cloth that tore, and of the Sanzer Rav's remark about the face of one who has an excuse. He explains that Heaven helps one who truly wants to come on time, and that a shogeg brings a korban because the excuse itself shows a lack of care.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the mitzvah to speak of Hashem's wonders and then shows them in nature: the measured oxygen in the air, the renewal of the body's cells, the blood and its clotting, and the expansion of matter in heat.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the mitzvah from divrei kabbalah to speak of all of Hashem's wonders, which brings a person to emunah, and with the Ramban in parshas Bo on the passuk about telling one's children. He asks why the chapters of Tehillim that praise Hashem are arranged by the alef-beis, and answers that one can never finish His praises; David ends only because the letters end, as the Gemara shows about the one who added praises in his tefillah. He then sets out to accustom the bachurim to see wonders everywhere. He describes how plants and animals exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide so that the air holds a measured amount of oxygen; how the body's cells are constantly replaced while the brain cells stay, which keeps memory; how the blood feeds the body, carries away waste and clots at a cut; and how matter expands with heat, as in a thermometer and in railway tracks.

en: Speaking of Hashem's wonders is a mitzvah from divrei kabbalah, and it brings a person to emunah.
The chapters of Tehillim that praise Hashem follow the alef-beis because His praises have no end; David stops only because the letters run out.
The Mashgiach wants the bachurim to grow used to seeing that the whole world, every tree, flower and stream, is full of Hashem's wonders.
Plants give off oxygen and animals give off carbon dioxide, and Hashem keeps the air at a measured amount of oxygen, neither too little to breathe nor so much that everything would burn.
The body's cells are constantly replaced, so that every seven years a person has a new body, but the brain cells are not renewed, and so memory lasts.
Hashem placed in the blood of every living creature a substance that seals a cut on contact with air; without it a person would bleed to death from a small cut.

title.en: The mitzvah to speak of Hashem's wonders

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the mitzvah to speak of Hashem's wonders and the Ramban in parshas Bo, asks why the chapters of praise in Tehillim follow the alef-beis, and answers that His praises never end. He announces that he will speak of wonders in nature so the bachurim grow used to seeing them everywhere.

title.en: Oxygen and the balance of the air

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every moving creature needs oxygen while plants, which do not move, need carbon dioxide; plants give off oxygen and animals give off carbon dioxide. Hashem keeps the air at a measured share of oxygen: less would choke all life, more would let a single fire burn the whole world.

title.en: The cells of the body and the brain

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the tiny cells that make up every living thing and how they are constantly worn out and replaced, so that every seven years a person has a new body, which helps one understand gilgul. Only the brain cells are not renewed, for otherwise a person could not remember beyond seven years; everything is made with a reckoning.

title.en: The blood and how it stops a cut

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the blood brings food and oxygen to every part of the body and carries away carbon dioxide like a sanitation system. He then explains the substance in the blood that dries on contact with air and seals a cut; without it the heart would pump out all the blood from the smallest cut.

title.en: Water, heat and expansion

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls water a wondrous thing and first sets out the rule that every material expands when warm and shrinks when cold. He explains a mercury thermometer by this rule and begins to describe railway tracks.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the place of Shmuel Hanavi is the place of Rosh Hashanah, since there Chana, who was remembered on Rosh Hashanah, revealed the ways of tefillah and was answered with Shmuel, the first of the prophets.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach suggests that just as each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a mitzvah, the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah: the haftarah of Rosh Hashanah tells of Chana, who conceived Shmuel on the day called 'haras olam'. All the laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, including davening quietly and lengthening one's prayer, which Eli did not know; tefillah, the Mashgiach notes, is something people belittle. He brings a Midrash that reads 'barren' as barren in tefillah and in Torah, and says the place is a segulah for one who struggles to daven or learn. Shmuel's first prophecy punished Chofni and Pinchas for holding back the women's return home. Chana was the first to use the name Tzevakos, praying for children. Finally, citing the Chasam Sofer, he says Chana's prayer in Shiloh was on Rosh Hashanah, and closes with blessings for the coming year.

en: Each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a mitzvah, and the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, alongside the Beis Hamikdash, just as milah has a place both in Chevron and in Shechem.
Rosh Hashanah is 'hayom haras olam', the day the world is conceived anew, and here Chana conceived Shmuel, the first of the prophets, on that very day.
All the laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, among them davening quietly and lengthening one's prayer, both of which Eli did not know.
The place of Shmuel Hanavi is a segulah for one who struggles to daven or to learn, to bring forth fruit from his Torah and tefillah.
Chana was the first in history to call Hashem by the name Tzevakos, and she used it to pray for children.
Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh even on Rosh Hashanah, and it was then that Chana davened and was answered.

title.en: The place of Shmuel Hanavi as a place of Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that each place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a mitzvah, and suggests that the place of Shmuel Hanavi is a place of Rosh Hashanah, alongside the Beis Hamikdash, as milah has places in both Chevron and Shechem. Rosh Hashanah is 'haras olam', and here Chana conceived Shmuel, the first of the prophets.

title.en: The laws of tefillah learned from Chana

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that many laws of tefillah are learned from Chana, such as standing before the King in Shemoneh Esrei. Eli thought her drunk because he did not know one davens quietly, nor that lengthening one's prayer is a virtue; tefillah, the Mashgiach says, is among the things people belittle.

title.en: Barren in tefillah and Torah: a segulah of the place

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions that they davened at Shmuel Hanavi that day and that Chana taught long prayer. He brings a Midrash that reads 'barren' as barren in tefillah and Torah, prayer or learning that bears no fruit, and says the place is a segulah for one who struggles to daven or learn.

title.en: Shmuel's first prophecy and the name Tzevakos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shmuel's first prophecy was a punishment on Chofni and Pinchas, whose sin was delaying the women's offerings and so keeping them from home. He then shows that Chana was the first to use the name Tzevakos, which the Chassidic sefarim link to netzach and hod, the source of prophecy, and that she used it to pray for children.

title.en: Chana's prayer was on Rosh Hashanah; blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects 'v'hayah' to the month of Tishrei and brings from the Chasam Sofer that Elkanah and Chana came to Shiloh even on Rosh Hashanah, when Chana davened. He concludes that those who came to this place should take on the quality of Rosh Hashanah, of Chana and of Shmuel, and blesses all with a good year.

title.en: Niggun

summary.en: A niggun is sung, followed by a brief remark that it was sung in camp in the time of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz.

title.en: Closing

summary.en: The close of the gathering.

catalogTitle: המשך ביאור לבטל הטענות כנגד מי שאומרים כ"ב שאין כל עבירה כע"ז ממש' מצוה ועבירה הם נצחיות.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 25, the Mashgiach explains why every aveirah is really like avodah zarah, why the hidden love of every Jew makes overcoming the yetzer hara near and easy, and why the claim 'I can do teshuvah later' fails, since a mitzvah and an aveirah are stamped into eternity.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach announces that he will now go to the essence of Tanya, which speaks even to plain people of a very low generation like ours. He recalls that all mitzvos branch out of 'Anochi' and 'Lo yihyeh', and that every Jew, even the simplest, instinctively gives his life rather than worship avodah zarah. Since every aveirah places a person under the sitra achra, it is a hidden form of avodah zarah; sinning anyway is the 'ruach shtus' Chazal learn from the sotah. In chapter 25 he distinguishes faulty reasoning from plain forgetting, and teaches that the remedy is to arouse the hidden love, illustrated by the Avnei Nezer's explanation about a kohenes. The love includes fear, like a mother holding her baby. He answers the argument of later teshuvah: above time nothing is temporary, so an aveirah is eternal. The same applies to positive mitzvos, and he closes with the darkness of the Shovevim weeks.

en: Every Jew, even the simplest, is instinctively ready to give his life rather than worship avodah zarah, without being trained for it.
Any aveirah, even a small rabbinic one, places a person under the jurisdiction of the sitra achra and is a subdivision of avodah zarah.
One sins either out of 'shtus', faulty reasoning, or out of 'shikchah', simply not thinking; the remedy is to remember and arouse the hidden love for Hashem.
The hidden love includes fear: one fears damaging the love, and it works as a G-dly instinct beyond reasoning.
The plea 'I will do teshuvah afterwards' fails, since a Jew would not worship avodah zarah even temporarily although teshuvah would help there too.
Above, there is no time, so an aveirah is not temporary; it is stamped into eternity, and the soul senses this.
The same reckoning applies to positive mitzvos: one must fight laziness, which comes from the element of earth, in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

title.en: Going to the essence of Tanya

summary.en: The Mashgiach says he will skip ahead to the core chapters of Tanya, which speak to plain people. He describes our generation as very low, with the signs Chazal give for the time before Moshiach, and says even so people like us can benefit from these chapters.

title.en: Mesirus nefesh for avodah zarah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that all mitzvos branch out of 'Anochi' and 'Lo yihyeh', and that every Jew, even the simplest, gives his life rather than serve avodah zarah, unlike soldiers or terrorists who must be trained. Yet every aveirah is a subdivision of avodah zarah, as the Ba'al Shem Tov says.

title.en: The sotah and the spirit of folly

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one sins only when a spirit of folly enters him, learned from the sotah, and builds the kal vachomer: one ready to die for avodah zarah should surely bear a small discomfort to avoid any aveirah, which is the same avodah zarah in disguise.

title.en: Folly, forgetting and the hidden love

summary.en: Starting chapter 25, the Mashgiach distinguishes two settings of sin: faulty reasoning (shtus) and simply not thinking (shikchah). The remedy is to remember and arouse the hidden love, since a person who sins forgets his bond with Hashem, like the sotah who forgets her bond with her husband.

title.en: The Avnei Nezer on the kohenes

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the case of a kohenes who remarried on the word of one witness and whose husband returned. The Avnei Nezer explains that a bond like chassan and kallah exists between every Jew and Hashem, felt more strongly by Shevet Levi, so she should have sensed her husband was alive.

title.en: Love that includes fear, a G-dly instinct

summary.en: On 'in your mouth and in your heart', the Mashgiach explains that the hidden love includes fear, like a mother holding her baby tightly on the stairs, and works as a G-dly instinct, like an animal giving itself for its offspring. So a person can surely break a small desire; and he notes that love is the root of positive mitzvos and fear of negative ones.

title.en: The plea of later teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach takes up the argument that a small aveirah can be fixed with teshuvah, and brings the Gemara that one who says 'I will sin and repent' is not given the means to repent. He explains that this means no heavenly arousal is sent, but if the person pushes his way in, the teshuvah still helps.

title.en: No 'temporary' above time

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that even with avodah zarah a person could do teshuvah afterwards, yet every Jew gives his life rather than be cut off even temporarily. The reason is that above there is no time, so an aveirah is stamped into eternity, and the soul feels it would lose its eternity.

title.en: Fighting laziness in positive mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the same reckoning to positive mitzvos, with the example of missing Mincha for a ball game. Laziness comes from the element of earth, the most passive element, and one must fight it with strength in Torah, tefillah and tzedakah, the three pillars.

title.en: Victory removes the concealment

summary.en: The Mashgiach says overcoming the yetzer hara is near and possible for everyone, and after victory the concealment is lifted and one feels close to Hashem. He explains 'Hashem Echad': no place is empty of Hashem, and the darkness of this world is only a blanket covering Him.

title.en: Shovevim: piercing the dark curtain

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects this to the Shovevim weeks, the darkest season, when the work is to pierce the dark curtain and find Hashem within it. Chanukah prepares for it; today the darkness has entered our homes, and in these weeks of reading about the exodus one should extricate one's own soul from Mitzrayim.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches the bachurim that every day and every tefillah is a new creation with its own tikkunim, so the beginning of the day, of davening and of learning must be sanctified, down to a person's first word, thought, sight and even his Jewish name.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to his warning against talking before davening, allowing only kind and holy words, and tells the bachurim to daven slowly and with their yeshiva. He describes davening as an ascent through the worlds of Asiyah, Yetzirah and Beriah up to Shemoneh Esrei before the King, and a descent that brings the shefa down, each step marked by a Kaddish, so parts should not be skipped as a habit. He speaks of the higher Shabbos davening and of a chazzan who must lift the tzibbur, with a story of the Sanzer Rav. Every day, he explains, is a new world with new tikkunim, so a missed tefillah cannot be made up. The beginning carries the whole act, as with writing a Sefer Torah lishmah, learning and davening. Therefore Modeh Ani is said at once, the first sight should be holy, and a Jew should be called by his Jewish name, which holds his shlichus.

en: The Mashgiach says the first words of the day should be words before Hashem, and talking before Shacharis takes away the help from Heaven to daven well.
Davening rises through the worlds up to Shemoneh Esrei and then brings the shefa down; each passage is marked by a Kaddish, so one should not skip parts as a habit.
Every day is a new creation with its own task, so every tefillah does tikkunim that no other tefillah can do, and a missed davening cannot be made up.
The intention stated at the beginning carries through the whole act, as with writing a Sefer Torah, learning and davening, so one should say at the start that he is doing it for the mitzvah.
On waking, the first word, thought, act and sight should be devoted to Hashem: Modeh Ani at once, before washing, and a look at the tzitzis or mezuzah.
Each Jew has his own shlichus, alluded to in his name, so he should be called by his Jewish name, which strengthens his soul, and not by a non-Jewish name, which strengthens the sitra achra.
